lead.topic: Striking EEB paper: long-term asexuality and phylogenetic reconstruction
lead.headline: Ancient asexuality can scramble a family tree
lead.deck: A ladder-shaped planarian phylogeny reflects unusual biology.
lead.authors: Benítez-Álvarez L, Tenaguillo-Arriola I, Leria L, Fernández R, Riutort M
paragraphs: A family tree usually groups individuals from the same population together. Earlier work on Dugesia, a genus of freshwater planarians, found something stranger: asexual individuals appeared separately on long branches, forming a ladder. These animals reproduce by fission, splitting into pieces that regenerate. The pattern raised a basic question. Had the reconstruction method been fooled, or had a long history without sexual reproduction changed the genetic signal itself? The answer matters because researchers routinely use branching trees to infer how populations and species are related.

Lisandra Benítez-Álvarez and colleagues revisited the problem using transcriptomes, which sample expressed genes, and nuclear markers. They compared phylogenetic analyses with genetic variation within individuals and examined explanations involving prolonged asexuality or hybridization. The authors report that the ladder persists as a biological signal. Comparisons with other fission-reproducing planarians support an ancient history, while retained ancestral genetic variants obscure the relationships that conventional trees try to recover. The study therefore connects a question about asexual survival to a practical problem in evolutionary inference: a tidy tree model can misrepresent a complicated genetic history.
lead.push: The next step is to ask how reliably competing histories can be distinguished. Simulations that vary the age of asexuality, ancestral diversity and hybrid ancestry could reveal when a ladder is diagnostic and when it is ambiguous. That would turn an intriguing pattern into a test with known limits.

people.name: Lisandra Benítez-Álvarez
people.bio: Lisandra Benítez-Álvarez is listed as a laboratory technician in the Multicellgenome Lab at the Institute of Evolutionary Biology (CSIC-UPF). Her 2022 doctoral thesis at the Universitat de Barcelona examined diversification and dispersal in planarians, moving from individual genes to much larger genetic datasets. Her research connects molecular variation with evolutionary history.

people.name: Marta Riutort
people.bio: Marta Riutort is a full professor of genetics at the Universitat de Barcelona. Her Planarian Diversity and Evolution Lab studies how genetic variation reveals the origins and distributions of freshwater and terrestrial flatworms. Its work spans phylogeny, biodiversity and genomic data, with collaborations extending to seabirds and whales.

slot2.headline: Local rules build a world of shells
slot2.body: Molluscs build an astonishing range of shells by adding material at the growing edge. Huan Liu and Kaushik Bhattacharya asked how a local growth rule could generate these entire shapes. Their model repeats a fixed rule that depends only on the edge's geometry. Mathematically, the resulting shell is traced by a Lie group, a continuous family of transformations, acting on the larval shell. The authors describe nearly all known shell forms with three ingredients: a scale, an orientation vector, and the initial edge curve. Relating these ingredients to a phylogeny gives a compact way to compare shell shapes and their evolution.

slot3.headline: One positron becomes a precision physics laboratory
slot3.cite: Myers TG, Soucy L, Sukra BAD, Sinha B, Gabrielse G, Physical Review Letters, 2026, 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj; Viewpoint in Physics
slot3.body: A single positron, the electron's antimatter counterpart, can now be controlled one quantum jump at a time. Researchers at Northwestern University trapped a positron for months, cooled its motion, and detected changes in its cyclotron motion and spin without destroying it. The apparatus holds the particle inside a microwave cavity, which slows the decay of excited states enough to measure them. This is a platform for a future precision measurement, not that measurement itself. Comparing positron and electron magnetic moments could test CPT symmetry, which predicts equal magnitudes and opposite signs. The team opens a route to much sharper tests.
